entities.label: Institution
entities.summary:
Brown University, founded in 1764 in Providence, Rhode Island, is one of America's eight Ivy League universities and the first American institution of higher education to explicitly reject religious tests for admission, establishing a tradition of academic freedom that influenced American higher education. Brown was the first college to accept students regardless of religious affiliation — its 1764 charter specifying that no student shall be 'debarred admission' for religious reasons — a revolutionary principle in colonial America.

Brown was founded as Rhode Island College, reflecting Rhode Island's tradition as a haven for religious dissent (Roger Williams founded the colony on principles of religious liberty). Renamed for Nicholas Brown Jr. in 1804 after a major donation, the university developed a distinctive model: no core curriculum, student-designed programs, and unusual curricular freedom. These features were codified in the 1969 'New Curriculum' reforms that made Brown famous for student choice and academic experimentation.

Brown's Pembroke College for women (founded 1891) was merged with Brown in 1971 creating a fully coeducational institution. Brown's open curriculum — no required courses — attracts students seeking intellectual freedom and self-direction. The university's medical school, engineering program, and Watson Institute for International Studies maintain research excellence. Notable alumni include seven Amer presidents' children, John D. Rockefeller Jr., and author Emma Goldman.
